description: We are NebulaeX, a team of passionate innovators, developers, and problem-solvers driven by curiosity and a shared interest in space technology. We aim to combine creativity, AI, programming, and emerging technologies to develop innovative solutions to real-world challenges in the space sector. We welcome enthusiastic teammates skilled in Python, AI/ML, web development, data science, UI/UX, and problem-solving who are ready to explore beyond boundaries and build something extraordinary.
summary:
We developed Sol-9, an open-source, full-stack astronomical web platform designed to uncover Planet X candidates, ultracool brown dwarfs, and variable stars using data from NASA’s SPHEREx all-sky survey.

To address the challenge, Sol-9 couples NASA/IPAC IRSA SIA2 cutouts with a 60-FPS HTML5 time-series blinking engine inspired by WiseView. It automatically aligns multi-epoch exposures onto a common WCS footprint, computes Epoch-minus-Reference difference frames to reveal moving objects as high-contrast dipoles, and overlays ESA Gaia DR3 proper-motion vectors alongside CSA NEOSSat asteroid tracks. Users can click any pixel to perform instant 102-band aperture photometry (0.75–5.0 µm) to detect diagnostic methane, water vapor, and carbon monoxide absorption features.

This project is important because extracting discoveries from petabyte-scale hyperspectral surveys requires bridging heavy scientific computing with intuitive visualization. By democratizing multi-epoch difference imaging and on-the-fly spectroscopy, Sol-9 empowers both professional astronomers and citizen scientists to explore the uncharted outer Solar System in search of our missing ninth planet.
details:
• What does your project do, and how does it work?

  • Sol-9 is a web-based astronomical observatory platform built to discover Planet X candidates, ultracool brown dwarfs, and variable stars in NASA’s SPHEREx all-sky survey.
  • It fetches multi-epoch near-IR cutouts from NASA/IPAC IRSA SIA2, applies sub-pixel WCS alignment, and calculates Epoch-minus-Reference difference frames so moving objects pop out as black-and-white dipoles on a 60-FPS canvas blinker.
  • Clicking any star triggers instant circular aperture photometry across all 100 active SPHEREx near-IR channels (0.75–5.0 µm) with automated molecular detection.

• What benefits does it have?

  • Zero-Install Web Access: Eliminates heavy multi-gigabyte FITS downloads; anyone can explore NASA datasets directly in a browser.
  • Dual Motion + Chemical Verification: Pairs astrometric motion (blinking dipoles) with atmospheric spectroscopy (methane and water detection) to eliminate false positives in seconds.
  • Instantaneous Performance: Asynchronous parallel querying and disk caching deliver sub-second load times.

• What is the intended impact?

  • Democratizes Citizen Astronomy: Empowers students and amateur astronomers worldwide to actively hunt for outer Solar System bodies, inspired by NASA's Backyard Worlds.
  • Accelerates Discovery: Equips professional researchers with fast screening, multi-mission overlays, and one-click data exports (CSV, JSON, PNG).

• What tools did you use?

  • Frontend: React 18, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, HTML5 Canvas, Aladin Lite v3 (WebAssembly), Plotly.js.
  • Backend: Python 3.12, FastAPI, Astropy, Astroquery, Reproject, Photutils, NumPy, SciPy, Pillow, DiskCache.
  • Data Sources: NASA/IPAC IRSA (SPHEREx & AllWISE), ESA Gaia DR3, CSA NEOSSat via CADC.
  • DevOps: Docker, Docker Compose.

• How is your project creative?

  • First Blinker + Spectroscopy Hybrid: While classic tools like WiseView only show grayscale motion, Sol-9 lets users click a moving candidate and immediately analyze its atmospheric chemistry.
  • Tri-Agency Space Integration: Synchronizes data from NASA, ESA, and the Canadian Space Agency into a single coordinate reticle.
  • Browser HDR Math: Implements Lupton Asinh stretching and difference imaging on the fly to reveal faint targets without saturating bright stars.

• What factors did your team consider?

  • Network Fault Tolerance: Enforced strict 2-second timeouts and multi-threaded parallel queries so remote server lags never freeze the user interface.
  • Human Visual Pattern Recognition: Engineered smooth 1–20 FPS stepper controls, dipole subtraction, and false-color RGB composites to help the human eye spot moving signals.
  • Scientific Rigor: Adhered strictly to NASA/IPAC tutorial standards, calibrated WCS headers, and standard astronomical flux units (mJy).
